newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai bond default seen swaying creditor sentiment.
newsitem.headline: Thai bond default seen swaying creditor sentiment.

text.p: The unprecedented default by property firm Somprasong Land on a Euro-convertible bond is set to increase nervousness in an already fragile market for Thai debt, fixed income analysts said on Thursday.
Somprasong failed to make a $3.1 million interest payment on an $80 million Euro-convertible in February.
Bondholders meeting in London earlier this week overwhelmingly rejected a settlement offer from the firm and decided to call a default on the paper.

"Being the first default by a Thai company on an international security it will be monitored very carefully, and it certainly doesn't do any good for sentiment," said Florian Schmidt, head of debt syndication at Nomura International in Hong Kong.

The firm's future, and the outcome for the bondholders, is now highly uncertain as the bond's trustee Bankers Trust is expected to take the untried step of taking the matter before Thai courts, analysts said.
That threatens an efficiency test of a Thai legal system ill-equipped to handle the case, they added.
"What the bondholders are trying to do is push the company into some kind of bankruptcy procedure," said Juanita Mayr, a credit analyst at Salomon Brothers in Hong Kong.
"But there is absolutely no bankruptcy law in Thailand. After a company has defaulted on its payments they don't do anything, and the whole thing could take for ever," Mayr said.

There are also concerns that senior creditors, which include some major local financial institutions, have begun cherry picking Somprasong assets and may continue to do so while a bondholders' settlement takes years to grind through the local courts.
The process of a Somprasong settlement now threatens to further unnerve creditors already rocked by Thailand's deepest economic crisis for more than decade, analysts said.
Most concerned are those holding paper linked to other struggling property firms or companies with high U.S. dollar exposure as the recently floated Thai baht continues to weaken, they added.
It will also help eliminate new Thai debt issues in a market already shutting its doors to even the highest quality new Thai corporate credits, they added.

"The market is virtually closed even for the big ones. This is not just a matter of credit or spread, this is a matter of whether there are lines available and most of the banks have virtually shut down their exposure to Thailand," Schmidt said.
"There are no more lines from Hong Kong and Singapore, and in Europe...nobody touches Thailand anyway," he added.
